So BPA is a plasticizer (or antioxident) in these packages. From my understanding of how the diffusion of plasticizers works (and please somebody correct me if I am wrong), there will be a layer of BPA at the surface that can evaporate or leach into any material it contacts. However, the rate at which this happens is incredibly slow. How slow exactly? Not sure, could try to find a paper on it but sufficive to say we can estimate it based on things like vapor pressure (controls release into atmosphere) and H2O solubility (should be related to how easily it can get into skin/food).

So the vapor pressure is exceedingly low (10^-8 mmHg) which means almost none of it will evaporate into the air and will therefore only be able to get into the food by direct contact.

The water solubility is <300 ppm, which is not very water soluble so it has no reason to want to be in food/skin.

So again, either it would need to diffuse through the polymer matrix to the surface and sublimate as a gas (almost impossible) or diffuse through a contact interface into water/food(which is still basically water) and it can only do that at up to 300 ppm. Also it's still pretty unlikely it will be entropically favorable to be in a big mac/fries.

So please somebody correct me if I am wrong but I am calling this a clickbaity title about a chemical that some people are afraid of for little to no reason.

This study on BPA as found in receipt paper I thought was informative and shows different rates of absorption. I would be curious what you think of it: http://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0110509

I'll take a look tonight or tomorrow. I usually work with DOP+PS so BPA+PC is a bit otuside what I normally look at and I am about the polymers, not medicine but I will take a look.

E: This deals with direct contact under very specific circumstances. More to come.

E3: NOt the most relevant paper to my arguments but here is what they say and what I think.

If you have wet hands (wetted with hand sanitizer) BPA absorbs much more quickly. Worth noting, the total amount of BPA on the hands never exceeds 10 ug whereas the amount on the receipts is about 20 mg/receipt. The do normalize this to an area cross section which reduces it to 9 mg/area. So really when you touch a receipt for a long time with dry hands something like .1% of the total BPA you contact is adsorbed onto your hand.

Mind you this says nothing (yet) about rates of adsorption into the body. They speculate that the decrease in BPA levels on the wet hands (ones that used hand sanitizer designed to facilitate absorption) after 45 seconds is due to adsorption.

So then they did another experiment. They said, what if you use hand sanitizer at McDonalds (or wherever) THEN immediately ate some food (french fries), what happens? They took a urine sample to determine total BPA adsorbed and basically saw ng levels of BPA present. So if we assume that the average person at McDonalds eats the equivalent of 100 fries then you might get 1 ug of BPA adsorbed from this entire process.

Now the rest of their work was in isolating the relative contributions of BPA adsorption. How much was adsorbed through skin on the hand versus through the tongue vs through digestion. They conclude that dermal absorption is more prevalent than previously thought, which means maybe try not to hold the receipt too long.

So I have a few comments about the paper as well. I may have missed it but I am not sure exactly how they controlled contact area for the subjects, which can introduce additional error. The number of subjects is also very small, though the results seem reasonably sound. Finally, we must remember this experiment was designed to maximize exposure and the levels seen were overall less than a few ug total. The bigger problem is if somebody touches 20 or 100 receipts per day (cashiers be warned).

Now, the original article, though mentioning BPA, actually discusses phthalates (I specifically look at DOP in PS -- not mentioned in original article but whatevs.) such as DOP (Dioctyl Phthalate). Again, the recent work they are reporting on is phthalate exposure in the general population. So what is causing this? Well actually a similar mechanism as the BPA exposure in that paper. People are touching things with large amounts of low MW phthalates which are being absorbed. But it's not just fast food; personal care products, solvents, adhesives, and medications are all mentioned in the original papers first paragraph.

So at this point I will save you from my analysis of another medical paper (I'm a physics person I worry about how these molecules move in my sample and how much is lost, spoiler: Below Tg (80 C for PVC which is what the article addresses) next to none. Near Tg not a heck of a lot, above Tg slightly more). What does this mean? If you buy a sandwich that comes in a plastic package, if that package is rigid it is going to lose almost none of the plasticizer, especially if it is plasticized with a higher MW phthalate (check out the wiki page on plasticizers I update it from time to time and it has some ok information).

Over all the article OP linked seems to be mostly anti BPA fear mongering. Is BPA bad for you? Probably, so is red meat according to some studies. Should be aware of it? Yes. Should you eat your receipt? No, obviously not. Should you not buy that water bottle because it has BPA in it? No, it's probably fine. Are phthalates bad for you? Yes. Are you getting significant amounts of phthalates from your fast food? No way, the concentration of phthalates found in the general population never exceeds 1ug/ml. By contrast, despite wearing glove/goggles/lab coat and frankly not spilling anything on myself, on a day that I work with DOP the concentration in my body probably can reach 10s of ug/mol and it's still probably fine (that being said DOP is relatively high MW).

Finally, I want to comment on the article OP cited. They had 4 citations and I thank them for showing them at the bottom. BUT they cited one new paper that dealt with phthalates (actually no they cited the daily mail who cited nothing except an author comment and the journal it's published in), 2 articles form their own site that talk about BPA replacements and BPA toxicity, and a citation I cannot find. They don't have a coherent argument that there is some new revelation. They are arguing becuase BPA can be adsorbed by eating after contacting BPA coated paper therefore BPA can be adsorbed into your fast food because fast food containers contain similar plasticizers... Not totally sure but I think they just crammed 3 papers together to scare off people. The title "It's not just in the meal, but the packaging: BPA toxicity in fast food packaging could lead to high rates of brain defects" is completely misleading.

The study's authors tested 14 different BPA-free plastic resins, the raw materials used to make plastic products, and found that four of them released chemicals that mimic the female hormone estrogen. That's not surprising. As Mother Jones reported earlier this year, many BPA-free plastic goods—from baby bottles and sippy cups to food-storage containers—leach potentially harmful estrogenlike chemicals. But until now, it wasn't clear what role the resins played. The new study suggests that sometimes the resins themselves are part of the problem, though additives such as dyes and antioxidants can make it worse.

In the case of polystyrene, the resin used in styrofoam and similar products, the authors tested 11 samples and consistently found estrogen seepage after exposure to intense steam or ultraviolet rays.

Styrofoam is a registered trademark of Dow. The company stresses that its product is used for crafts and building insulation rather than food and beverage containers. ("There isn't a coffee cup, cooler, or packaging material in the world made from actual Styrofoam," according to Dow's website.) But generic polystyrene foam, which most people call styrofoam anyway, is ubiquitous in the food services industry, where its found in everything from meat trays to takeout containers. Polystyrene resin—which the Environmental Protection Agency has labeled a suspected carcinogen—is also used to make hard plastic items, including utensils and toothbrushes.
